verdict: Devon's first full quarter after merging with Coterra made it a much bigger producer — revenue jumped 58% to $6.9B — but a $914M hedging loss held reported profit to $1.0B.

kpis.label: Revenue growth
kpis.note: Revenue $6.9B, vs $4.3B a year ago — first full quarter after the Coterra merger

kpis.label: EPS (GAAP diluted)
kpis.note: Core EPS was $1.42, excluding hedging and deal items

kpis.label: Production
kpis.note: Thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day; oil was 553,000 barrels a day

segments.name: Oil, gas & NGL sales (after hedging)
segments.note: Selling oil ($85.63 benchmark price), natural gas and natural gas liquids (NGLs — propane, butane and similar). The $5,939M of sales is shown after $914M of hedging losses — contracts that lock in prices lost value as prices rose; $729M of that loss is a non-cash revaluation. A year ago the same line, after a small hedging gain, was $2,889M.

segments.name: Marketing & midstream
segments.note: Gathering, processing and selling other producers' oil and gas, and pipeline services. Revenue rose 27%, though the costs of this business ($1,855M) roughly match what it brings in.

opex.name: Marketing & midstream expenses
opex.note: The cost of buying, gathering and transporting oil and gas for the marketing business — it roughly offsets that segment's revenue.

opex.name: Depreciation, depletion & amortization
opex.note: Spreading the cost of wells and reserves as the oil and gas is produced — a non-cash charge (DD&A). It roughly doubled with the Coterra merger.

opex.name: General & administrative
opex.note: Running the company — head office and support.

opex.name: Restructuring & transaction costs
opex.note: Costs of merging Devon with Coterra and restructuring afterwards.

opex.name: Exploration expenses
opex.note: Looking for new oil and gas — geological work and wells that did not pay off.

otherDetail: Other expense of $147M is financing costs, net: $150M of interest on debt, less $7M of interest income, plus $4M of other financing costs.
footerNote: Adaptation for an oil and gas producer: production expenses (lease operating expense, gathering/processing/transportation and production and property taxes, as detailed in Devon's supplemental tables) are the cost of revenue; financing costs are shown below operating income, so operating income here is $1,399M before those financing costs. Hedging (derivative) results are netted inside the oil, gas and NGL sales segment so segment revenue stays positive and sums to total revenue.
oneTimers: Oil, gas and NGL derivatives lost $914M in the quarter — $185M of cash settlements paid out plus a $729M non-cash drop in the contracts' value as prices rose. Excluding hedging swings, deal costs and impairments, core earnings were $1,633M ($1.42 per share) vs reported $1,008M ($0.88).

Devon agreed on October 8 to sell its Eagle Ford assets for $4.2B in cash (about $3.5B after tax and adjustments), closing expected in early 2027 — the proceeds are earmarked for bigger buybacks and debt reduction.

takeaways.title: The merger doubled the company
takeaways.text: This was the first full quarter of the combined Devon–Coterra. Production averaged 1,668,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day (oil 553,000 barrels a day), up from 853,000 a year ago, and revenue rose 58% to $6.9B.

takeaways.title: Hedges capped the oil-price upside
takeaways.text: Devon locks in future prices with hedging contracts (insurance against price falls). With benchmark oil at $85.63, those contracts lost $914M — mostly a $729M non-cash revaluation — cutting reported EPS to $0.88 versus core EPS of $1.42.

takeaways.title: Eagle Ford sale funds returns
takeaways.text: Devon agreed to sell its Eagle Ford assets for $4.2B, retired the last $750M of its term loan (debt is $10.6B, heading for a $9B target), and plans buybacks of more than $1B in the fourth quarter alone.
